[[File:Nichols plot.svg|class=skin-invert-image|thumb|right|A Nichols plot.]]

The '''Nichols plot''' is a [[Plot (graphics)|plot]] used in [[signal processing]] and [[control theory|control design]], named after American engineer [[Nathaniel B. Nichols]].<ref>Isaac M. Howowitz, ''Synthesis of Feedback Systems'', Academic Press, 1963, Lib Congress 63-12033 p. 194-198</ref><ref>Boris J. Lurie and Paul J. Enright, ''Classical Feedback Control'', Marcel Dekker, 2000, {{ISBN|0-8247-0370-7}} p. 10</ref><ref>Allen Stubberud, Ivan Williams, and Joseph DeStefano, ''Shaums Outline Feedback and Control Systems'', McGraw-Hill, 1995, {{ISBN|0-07-017052-5}} ch. 17</ref> It plots the [[phase response]] versus the response magnitude of a [[transfer function]] for any given frequency, and as such is useful in characterizing a system's [[frequency response]].

==Use in control design==
Given a [[transfer function]],

:<math> G(s) = \frac{Y(s)}{X(s)} </math>

with the [[closed-loop transfer function]] defined as,

:<math> M(s) = \frac{G(s)}{1+G(s)} </math>

the Nichols plots displays <math> 20 \log_{10}(|G(s)|) </math> versus <math> \arg(G(s))</math>. Loci of constant <math> 20 \log_{10}(|M(s)|) </math> and <math> \arg(M(s))</math> (so-called [[Hall circles]]) are overlaid to allow the designer to obtain the closed loop transfer function directly from the open loop transfer function.  Thus, the frequency <math> \omega </math> is the parameter along the curve.  This plot may be compared to the [[Bode plot]] in which the two inter-related graphs - <math> 20 \log_{10}(|G(s)|) </math> versus <math> \log_{10}(\omega) </math> and <math> \arg(G(s))</math> versus <math> \log_{10}(\omega) </math>) - are plotted.

In [[control system|feedback control design]], the plot is useful for assessing the stability and robustness of a linear system.  This application of the Nichols plot is central to the [[Quantitative feedback theory|quantitative feedback theory (QFT)]] of Horowitz and Sidi, which is a well known method for robust control system design.

In most cases, <math> \arg(G(s))</math> refers to the phase of the system's response. Although similar to a [[Nyquist plot]], a Nichols plot is plotted in a [[Polar coordinate system]] while a Nyquist plot is plotted in a [[Cartesian coordinate system]].
